title: India–US trade deal: announced in February, still not signed
dek: A tariff cut was announced with fanfare. Nine months later, courts, new duties and a sanctions law have kept it in limbo.
bigLabel: US duty on most Indian goods since 24 Jul

glance.what: The US and India announced a deal in February to cut US tariffs on Indian goods to 18% from 50%. As of 3 November there is still no signed agreement.
glance.why: US tariffs decide how competitive Indian exports like textiles, gems, engineering goods and pharma are in India’s biggest export market.
glance.next: No public deadline. Some trade analysts say the US midterm results make an early interim deal more likely.

forYou: If you work in or invest in export-heavy sectors, the final tariff rate matters more than the headlines. Nothing announced is binding until a deal is signed.
next: No public deadline. Analysts expect movement after the US midterms.

events.title: Trump announces a deal: tariffs to 18% from 50%
events.summary: In return, India is to stop buying Russian oil and lower trade barriers for US goods.

events.title: Joint statement sets out a framework for an interim deal
events.summary: Both governments publish a framework for an interim agreement, with talks on a wider trade pact to follow.

events.title: US Supreme Court strikes down the legal basis for the tariffs
events.summary: In a 6–3 ruling, the court says the emergency-powers law (IEEPA) does not authorise tariffs. The US turns to other trade laws.

events.title: A new 10% duty on most Indian goods
events.summary: A Section 301 duty of 10% starts applying to most Indian imports into the US, becoming the main sticking point in talks.

events.title: US sanctions law threatens tariffs of up to 100%
events.summary: A new US law authorises tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, naming India and China as at direct risk.

events.title: Still no signed deal
events.summary: The 18% rate announced in February was never applied. After the US midterms, Indian trade analysts argue an early interim deal has become more likely.
